The Mountain wren (Troglodytes solstitialis) exhibits several life-history traits that align with its high-altitude Andean existence. Field records indicate that newly hatched nestlings have a wet weight at birth of approximately 1.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.5 grams], a value inferred from measurements on the closely related house wren Troglodytes aedon. This modest initial mass is typical of altricial passerines, which require intensive parental brooding and feeding during the early nestling period. For this species, incubation and the subsequent hatching event occur after an age at birth estimated at 13 days [ab = 13 days] when eggs are maintained at a steady 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a temperature regime that mirrors conditions within a well-insulated cavity nest. This incubation period is relatively brief compared to many other small-bodied songbirds, likely reflecting the thermal stability of the high-elevation nest microhabitat. The brevity of this embryonic stage is somewhat counterbalanced by a rapid post-hatching developmental trajectory, ensuring that chicks can fledge before the onset of the harsh winter conditions characteristic of their montane environment.

The fledging event, representing the age at which young birds first achieve sustained flight and leave the nest, occurs at 16 days after hatching [tx = 16 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This timing, based on comparative data from Troglodytes aedon, is relatively rapid and allows for multiple nesting attempts within the short austral summer. Following fledging, the juvenile period involves a continued dependence on parental provisioning as the pin-feathered chick develops into a fully independent bird. During this vulnerable phase, the growing individuals must rapidly accumulate body mass and refine their foraging skills to survive their first winter. The time to sexual maturation is delayed considerably beyond the fledging stage, as the young birds need to establish territories and acquire the physiological condition necessary for reproduction.

However, the age at which individuals actually engage in their first successful brood is considerably later. This low fecundity is typical of many high-elevation tropical passerines, which invest heavily in a few high-quality offspring rather than producing many young. The maximum recorded longevity for this species is approximately 8.8 years [am = approximately 8.8 years] when measured at the typical avian body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a lifespan that is remarkably long given the small body size of the Mountain wren. This extended lifespan may be an adaptation to the unpredictable and harsh environmental conditions of the Andes, allowing individuals multiple reproductive opportunities across several breeding seasons. The combination of a low annual fecundity and a long lifespan suggests that the Mountain wren employs a relatively slow life-history strategy, prioritizing adult survival and repeated breeding attempts over high immediate reproductive output.

The ultimate wet weight for females in this species is 11.4 grams [Wwi = 11.4 grams], a modest body mass that reflects the energetic constraints of a high-altitude lifestyle with low ambient oxygen availability. Additionally, the basal metabolic rate of this species has been measured at 49.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 49.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when maintained at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This metabolic rate is relatively elevated compared to other wrens of similar body size, likely representing a compensatory mechanism for the cold temperatures and reduced oxygen partial pressure at elevations above 2500 meters. The high surface-area-to-volume ratio of such a small bird necessitates a high BMR to maintain endothermy. This energetic demand also influences foraging behavior, as the species must continuously feed on arthropods throughout the day to meet its daily metabolic costs. These physiological traits, combined with the life-history parameters already described, contribute to a finely tuned adaptation to the unique challenges of the paramo and cloud forest ecosystems.
